doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: London: studio reputation, Brotherhood of Breath, Nottingham gig
summary: In England he was seen as a studio player, played with John Surman's Brotherhood of Breath, was left out of the Berlin festival, and worked Bryan Ferry and Nottingham dance gigs.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Right. I had two soprano saxophones that I sold. They were a hundred numbers apart. They were both Selmers, and I kick myself for dropping these things. One sounded like an English horn and the other one had a much bigger, more of a jazz soprano sound. So whenever people used to hire me I’d ask them what kind of sound they wanted and bring the appropriate instrument. I sold a really good clarinet. I sold a really good alto flute, a really good bass flute, and I kick myself all over the place for letting go of — but there is just so much plumbing you can carry when you’re changing countries. But England was okay. It was an entirely different scene. There was nothing much established. And the contacts that I had over there had known me as a studio player, and they weren’t. So when people were offering me jobs they’d say oh no, no, he’s a studio player. He’s not a jazz player. So I had to, just a minute, I had to do that. And there was also another odd faction in England. I was playing something for John Surman on a South African group called the Brotherhood of Breath. Very avante garde, you know, very violent kind of © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
music, but they were good players. Alan Skidmore was playing tenor on it. A wonderful alto player, an African alto player, named Dudu Pukwana.

He’s kind of like an African version of Ornette Coleman. Fabulous player. And so they were going to do the Berlin Jazz Festival. But they hadn’t mentioned anything to me about it. And I said, “so am I going to Berlin with you?” And they said, “no.” And I said, “oh, why?” They said, “oh because you sound too much like an American.” And I said, coming from New Zealand, “isn’t that the object?” They wanted somebody who didn’t have that American sound I guess I had.

I have no idea. I just didn’t go to Berlin with them. You know I didn’t play with them anymore. But I played with some of the newer avante garde, new age rocker kind of guys like Bryan Ferry. And I was holding down a six night a week gig in Nottingham of all places. I would have to drive from London and stay over a couple of nights and play and have just a big dance band. But we would just do all kinds of stuff.
Probably ’69, ’70. And I just got sick of that and one day I turned to my wife and said “I think it’s time we got out of here.” So we moved, burned a few bridges, and went to France.
